statusText: Mapped policy state: EA_ON. Tail risk 3% (low) with no Nasdaq-100 price path observable inside the CME weekend halt, against Stress of 73% (high) on an oil and long-end-yield backdrop that eased slightly as the weekend's open checkpoints resolved.
recommendation: Tail remains far below the block threshold, so the mapped policy state stays EA_ON. A narrow danger window is published across the 22:00Z CME reopen and the hour after it (00:00-02:00 Berlin on 5 October), where the published forecast Tail path reaches the WATCH band on gap and discontinuity risk rather than on observed structure.
headline: Nasdaq-100 carries a record close into the CME reopen while a reported OPEC+ rollover, the G7 release of up to 100 million barrels and a bounded Riyadh refinery fire ease Stress off its ceiling and leave Tail at its floor
body:
CME equity-index futures have been halted since Friday 21:00Z and reopen at 22:00Z on 4 October, so no Nasdaq-100 price path exists to assess and Tail stays at its structural floor of 3%. The last observed path was orderly two-way behaviour. The cash index traded to an all-time intraday high of 31,017.53 on Friday 2 October, fully retraced it, and finished at a record 30,807.93, up 1.00%, in the lower part of its 30,737.07-31,017.53 range. Nasdaq-100 futures told the same story: a 31,282.50 high against a 31,061.75 settlement, roughly 0.7% off the high, with VIX settling at 15.31, down 6.59%. A record high that is fully retraced into the close is the opposite of the shallow-pullback, repeated-extension structure that Tail measures.

Stress is marked down to 73% from the 79% published an hour earlier. The reason is specific rather than a drift lower: the weekend items that drove the previous ratchet from 52% to 79% have either resolved or been bounded. Reporting on 4 October indicates the core OPEC+ group settled on steady November quotas, which removes the supply-surprise channel from an unscheduled meeting whose timing had never been published. Separately, the G7 confirmed on 2 October a release of up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude over four months, coordinated through the International Energy Agency and frontloaded into the first 20 days, after US diesel reached a record 6.52 dollars a gallon on 22 September and inventories hit a record low of 107.9 million barrels. WTI fell 1.90% to 91.11 dollars on that news and touched a one-month low of 88.06 before recovering.

The Saudi-Houthi escalation is likewise better bounded than it was. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group struck an Aramco facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones; witnesses and news agencies reported flames and black smoke, and the Saudi-led coalition called the account misleading. Neither Saudi authorities nor Aramco have confirmed the cause, any damage, or any impact on production, refining or exports. What has become clearer is the scale of what is at stake at that specific site: the Riyadh refinery is a domestic facility of roughly 126,000 barrels a day, not export infrastructure, and Saudi export routing is reported running above 80% of East-West pipeline capacity at close to 6 million barrels a day. Even a confirmed outage there would be a long way from an index-level one-way driver.

What keeps Stress firmly in the high band is structural rather than new. The Strait of Hormuz has been largely closed to commercial shipping since 28 February, with over 150 tankers reported anchored outside it; Brent sits near 102.25 dollars, up about 58% year on year; and the Federal Reserve H.15 release dated 2 October shows the 2-year at 4.78%, the 5-year at 5.01%, the 10-year at 5.24% and the 30-year at 5.61%. The Iran channel is also genuinely two-sided, which argues against reading it as a one-way Tail driver: the USS Theodore Roosevelt strike group and the Makin Island amphibious unit are deploying, adding 9,000 to 10,000 troops to roughly 50,000 already in the region, while indirect talks continue through Qatari mediators and Iran has floated a seven-day roadmap for reopening Hormuz that Washington rejected.

The macro mix behind Friday's record close is stagflationary rather than directional. September payrolls rose only 29,000 against expectations above 80,000, unemployment ticked up to 4.2%, and July and August were revised down by a combined 60,000. That cut October Fed hike odds to roughly 17% on CME FedWatch from about 36% a week earlier, though a December hike remains priced and the Fed raised rates at its September meeting. The FOMC minutes from that meeting, due 18:00Z on 7 October, are the week's main scheduled risk and are the kind of multi-stage repricing event that warrants care. ISM Services at 14:00Z on 5 October is the first catalyst, and preliminary Michigan sentiment on 9 October is expected near 48.1 with inflation expectations at 4.6%.

The forecast therefore holds Tail between 3% and 6% through the closed Sunday hours, steps it to 10% in the final hour before the reopen, and raises it to 21% and 20%, inside the WATCH band, across the 22:00Z reopen and the hour after it. That elevation is gap and discontinuity risk conditional on an unknown first print, not observed structure, and a contained reopen that trades both sides of the 31,061.75 futures settlement would retire it quickly. The published decay afterwards assumes orderly two-way discovery; a gap that holds without meaningful retracement, a second leg after a failed retracement, or a confirmed Saudi export outage would each invalidate that assumption. The shared deterministic Finviz context file was stale by several days and only partially collected at assessment time, with its futures and calendar sections unavailable, so it contributed no current evidence and this assessment rests entirely on independently verified primary and reputable current sources.

Tail then steps to 10% in the final closed hour and is raised to 21% and 20%, inside the WATCH band, across the 22:00Z CME reopen and the hour after it, which together form the published danger window. forecastDetail.comment: Weekend CME halt since Friday 21:00Z leaves no Nasdaq-100 price path to score, so Tail holds at its 3% floor; the last observed session was two-way, with a record cash high fully retraced into the close.

Tail unchanged at 3% while Stress is lowered to 73% from the prior published 79%, because the reported OPEC+ steady-November outcome and the confirmed G7 release of up to 100 million barrels both resolved in a Stress-easing direction.

Stress eases to 72% as the oil channel is reassessed: WTI fell 1.90% to 91.11 dollars on Friday and touched a one-month low of 88.06 on the G7 reserve announcement, the opposite of a supply-shock impulse.

Tail stays at 3% with the Riyadh refinery fire bounded rather than resolved: about 126,000 barrels a day of domestic refining capacity, with Saudi export routing reported above 80% of East-West pipeline capacity and no official confirmation of damage.

Stress 71% and Tail 3% through the closed European afternoon; a Saudi or Aramco confirmation of damaged refining or export capacity before the 22:00Z reopen is the condition that would change this, and it has not occurred.

Tail ticks to 4% on reopen uncertainty alone as the halt shortens; the Iran channel is genuinely two-sided, with a rejected Iranian Hormuz reopening roadmap on one side and a third US carrier group deploying on the other.
